plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 5: Newton's Laws of Motion
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a two-part free-body construction, panels (a) and (b), each pairing a small pictorial sketch with an isolated force diagram at its left and a legend of symbol definitions at its right. Both sketches show the same tan incline sloping down to the left, a small salmon block labeled A resting on a larger block labeled B, and a cord running up the slope; a rounded outline circles block A in (a) and block B in (b). In (a), block A is reduced to a black dot on a dashed line standing for the incline surface, carrying four red vectors: N_BA perpendicular to and away from the surface, T up the slope, f_BA down the slope, and w_A vertically down. In (b), block B carries five: N_B perpendicular away from the incline, f_AB and f_B both up the slope, N_AB perpendicular and directed down into the incline, and w_B vertically down. The legends spell the symbols out, among them "N_BA = normal force exerted by B on A" and "f_B = friction force exerted by the incline plane on B". Stacking the two isolations invites comparison of the paired contact forces and the reversed friction directions. The construction demonstrates how to isolate stacked bodies touching two surfaces at once.

interactionPlan.concept: Isolating each of two stacked blocks on an incline shows that a free-body diagram contains only the forces acting ON that body, and that the contact forces between the blocks are Newton's third-law pairs pointing in opposite directions on different bodies.
elements: Panel (a) label and panel (b) label centered beneath each half of the figure
Tan-filled incline wedge in both panels, hypotenuse sloping down to the left, gray outline on the slope surface
Small salmon-colored block labeled 'A' resting on top of a larger tan block labeled 'B' on the incline surface (both panels, identical sketch)
Black cord running from block A up the slope to the upper right, representing the tension
Rounded gray highlight outline circling block A in panel (a); same outline circling block B in panel (b)
Panel (a) free-body diagram at left: black dot for block A on a dashed line representing the incline surface

Panel (a) red vectors from the dot: N_BA perpendicular to and away from the incline surface (up-left of vertical), T directed up the slope (to the upper right), f_BA directed down the slope (to the lower left), w_A vertically downward
Panel (b) free-body diagram at left: black dot for block B on a dashed line representing the incline surface

Panel (b) red vectors from the dot: N_B perpendicular away from the incline, f_AB up the slope, f_B up the slope (slightly longer, lower), N_AB perpendicular and directed into the incline (down-right), w_B vertically downward
Vector labels in bold with overhead arrows: N_BA, T, f_BA, w_A, N_B, f_AB, f_B, N_AB, w_B
Legend list at right of panel (a): w_A = weight of block A; T = tension; N_BA = normal force exerted by B on A; f_BA = friction force exerted by B on A

Legend list at right of panel (b): w_B = weight of block B; N_AB = normal force exerted by A on B; N_B = normal force exerted by the incline plane on B; f_AB = friction force exerted by A on B; f_B = friction force exerted by the incline plane on B
Dashed incline-surface reference line under each free-body dot

interactions.teaches: A free-body diagram contains only the forces acting on the one object you circled; clicking A or B in the sketch dims the other body and its diagram, so the learner sees the boundary of the isolated system.

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency of A on B
options: A tends to slide down the slope
A tends to slide up the slope
interactions.default: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The whole system
demo_steps.narration: Two blocks sit stacked on the incline, with a cord pulling block A up the slope. Before drawing any arrows, notice that A touches two things — the cord and block B — while B touches A and the incline.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Isolate block A
demo_steps.narration: Click block A: everything else fades, leaving only the four forces acting on A — the tension T up the slope, the normal force N_BA from B, the friction f_BA from B, and A's weight w_A.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Isolate block B
demo_steps.narration: Click block B instead. B feels five forces: its weight w_B, the incline's normal N_B and friction f_B, plus the normal N_AB and friction f_AB that block A presses back onto it. The tension never appears — the cord does not touch B.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The normal-force pair
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the normal pair: N_BA pushes A away from the surface while N_AB presses down into it with equal magnitude. They are equal and opposite, but they live on different free-body diagrams, so they never cancel each other.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The friction pair
demo_steps.narration: Now highlight the friction pair: f_BA on A points down the slope while f_AB on B points up the slope. Same contact surface, same magnitude, opposite directions, acting on two different bodies.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Reverse the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Flip the tendency so the cord wins and A tends to slide up over B. Every friction arrow reverses along its own surface — friction opposes relative sliding, so its direction is decided by the motion, not by the picture's geometry.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide up the slope

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Third-law partners like N_BA and N_AB are equal and opposite but always appear on different free-body diagrams — which is exactly why isolating one body at a time is the only way to keep them straight.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing identical layout: left third holds the free-body diagram, middle holds the pictorial sketch, right third holds the symbol legend as left-aligned lines of text. Panel label '(a)' and '(b)' centered under each. In each sketch a tan wedge fills the lower right with its hypotenuse running from upper right to lower left at about 25–30 degrees; a gray line marks the slope surface. On the slope sit a tan block B with a smaller salmon block A on top, both drawn tilted to match the slope, with a thin black cord leaving A up-slope to the upper right. A rounded gray capsule outline encircles block A in panel (a) and block B in panel (b) to mark the isolated body. Free-body diagrams: a black dot on a short dashed line drawn at the incline angle; all force vectors are bold red arrows radiating from the dot, labeled in bold with overhead vector arrows. Panel (a) has four arrows (normal perpendicular up-left, tension up-slope, friction down-slope, weight straight down); panel (b) has five (normal up from incline, two friction arrows up-slope, one normal pressing down-right into the surface, weight straight down). Legends in black serif-style text repeat each symbol with its verbal definition. Interaction styling: the non-isolated body and its arrows drop to ~20% opacity; highlighted third-law pairs glow in a saturated accent (e.g. orange/gold stroke with a connecting curved annotation labelled 'equal and opposite, different bodies'); reversing the sliding tendency rotates each friction arrow 180 degrees along the dashed surface line while leaving normals and weights unchanged.

- Click for isolating a body: the learner clicks block A or block B in the incline sketch, the selected block outline and its free-body diagram brighten while the other body fades, making clear that a free-body diagram includes only forces acting on the isolated object.
- Toggle between contact-force pairs: the learner switches between forces on A and forces on B, paired normal and friction arrows highlight in opposite directions on the two diagrams, making clear that third-law pairs act on different bodies.

authoredContext:
Two Blocks on an Inclined Plane Construct the free-body diagram for object A and object B in the figure. Assume that the rope pulls object A so that it slides upward, and that object B is sliding down the slope.

Solution We start by creating a diagram for the first object of interest. In the figure(a), object A is isolated (circled) and represented by a dot.

As noted in step 4 of the problem-solving strategy, we then construct the free-body diagram in the figure(b) using the same approach. Object B experiences two normal forces and two friction forces due to the presence of two contact surfaces. The interface with the inclined plane exerts external forces of NB and fB, and the interface with object B exerts the normal force NAB and friction fAB; NAB is directed away from object B, and fAB is opposing the tendency of the relative motion of object B with respect to object A.

(a) The free-body diagram for isolated object A. (b) The free-body diagram for isolated object B. Comparing the two drawings, we see that friction acts in the opposite direction in the two figures. Friction always acts opposite the direction of motion or intended motion. Because object A is moving to the right, friction by B must act to the left. Object B is moving to the left relative to B, so the friction by A on B is to the right. The friction force by object A on object B is the third law pair of the friction force by B on A, and therefore these two forces must be in opposite directions. Because object B is sliding down the incline, the friction force by the ramp must oppose it and act up the ramp.

Figure a shows two objects on an inclined plane, sloping down to the left. Object A is on top of object B. A free body diagram shows T pointing right and up, parallel to the plane, N subscript BA pointing left and up, perpendicular to the plane, f subscript BA pointing left and down, parallel to the plane and w subscript A pointing vertically down. W subscript A is weight of block A, T is tension, N subscript BA is normal force exerted by B on A, f subscript BA is friction force exerted by B on A. Figure b shows the objects on the slope in the same manner. A free body diagram has f subscript B and f subscript AB pointing right and up, parallel to the slope, N subscript B pointing left and up perpendicular to the slope, w subscript B pointing vertically down and N subscript AB pointing down and right, perpendicular to the slope. W subscript B is weight of block B, N subscript AB is normal force exerted by A on B, N subscript B is normal force exerted by the incline plane on B. f subscript AB is friction force exerted by A on B. f subscript B is friction force exerted by the incline plane on B.

We now include any force that acts on the body. Here, no applied force is present. The weight of the object acts as a force pointing vertically downward, and the presence of the cord indicates a force of tension pointing away from the object. Object A has one interface and hence experiences a normal force, directed away from the interface. The source of this force is object B, and this normal force is labeled accordingly. Since object B s sliding down and object A s sliding up with respect to the interface, so the friction fBA is directed downward parallel to the inclined plane.

discrepancies: All text (legend lines, vector symbols, panel captions) is rendered at 14 px inside a 900-unit viewbox that is scaled down to ~600 px, so the labels read noticeably smaller relative to the artwork than in the source, where the legend text is prominent and comfortably readable.

Weight vector w⃗_B is drawn tilted (direction ≈ (-0.16, 0.99)) rather than straight down; the source also slants it slightly, but the generated tilt combined with the slanted w⃗_A/w⃗_B pair weakens the 'gravity is vertical' cue.

Panel (b)'s sketch: the rounded gray 'system boundary' outline hugs block B only and block A sits noticeably offset above it, whereas in the source the outline encloses the whole B-block body with A resting flush on its top face; the A/B stacking contact looks slightly detached in the generated version.

Minor angular differences in the free-body arrows (e.g. f⃗_AB and f⃗_B in panel (b) are closer together than in the source, and T is somewhat shorter), so the fan of arrows is a bit more crowded than the original spread.
Extra explanatory chrome not in the source (gold third-law highlight bar, narration text, key-insight popup) — useful pedagogically but adds elements absent from the static figure.
evaluation.notes: A close and well-composed reproduction of both free-body panels with correct force sets, directions and legends, backed by genuinely useful interactions (isolate-a-body, third-law pair highlight, friction-reversal toggle, 6-step narrated player); main weaknesses are slightly undersized text and a few minor geometry/placement deviations (tilted w⃗_B, A/B contact in panel (b), crowded arrow fan).
action_items: Increase legend and vector-symbol font sizes (legend ~17-18, symbols ~16-17 in viewbox units) or shrink the viewbox height so text renders at a comfortable inline size matching the source's visual hierarchy.
Draw w⃗_B (and w⃗_A) straight vertical, offsetting only the text label, so the weight arrows are unambiguously gravitational.
Reposition block A in panel (b) so its lower face sits flush on block B's top face along the incline, and size the rounded boundary outline to match the source's enclosure of the B body.
Widen the angular separation between f⃗_AB and f⃗_B in panel (b) and lengthen T in panel (a) to match the source's arrow spread and relative magnitudes.

plan.concept: Isolating each of two stacked blocks on an incline shows that a free-body diagram contains only the forces acting ON that body, and that the contact forces between the blocks are Newton's third-law pairs pointing in opposite directions on different bodies.

interactions.teaches: A free-body diagram contains only the forces acting on the one object you circled; clicking A or B in the sketch dims the other body and its diagram, so the learner sees the boundary of the isolated system.

interactions.label: Relative sliding tendency of A on B
options: A tends to slide down the slope
A tends to slide up the slope
interactions.default: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The whole system
demo_steps.narration: Two blocks sit stacked on the incline, with a cord pulling block A up the slope. Before drawing any arrows, notice that A touches two things — the cord and block B — while B touches A and the incline.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Isolate block A
demo_steps.narration: Click block A: everything else fades, leaving only the four forces acting on A — the tension T up the slope, the normal force N_BA from B, the friction f_BA from B, and A's weight w_A.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Isolate block B
demo_steps.narration: Click block B instead. B feels five forces: its weight w_B, the incline's normal N_B and friction f_B, plus the normal N_AB and friction f_AB that block A presses back onto it. The tension never appears — the cord does not touch B.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The normal-force pair
demo_steps.narration: Highlight the normal pair: N_BA pushes A away from the surface while N_AB presses down into it with equal magnitude. They are equal and opposite, but they live on different free-body diagrams, so they never cancel each other.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: The friction pair
demo_steps.narration: Now highlight the friction pair: f_BA on A points down the slope while f_AB on B points up the slope. Same contact surface, same magnitude, opposite directions, acting on two different bodies.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide down the slope

demo_steps.title: Reverse the sliding tendency
demo_steps.narration: Flip the tendency so the cord wins and A tends to slide up over B. Every friction arrow reverses along its own surface — friction opposes relative sliding, so its direction is decided by the motion, not by the picture's geometry.

state.slidingTendency: A tends to slide up the slope

plan.keyInsight: Third-law partners like N_BA and N_AB are equal and opposite but always appear on different free-body diagrams — which is exactly why isolating one body at a time is the only way to keep them straight.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing identical layout: left third holds the free-body diagram, middle holds the pictorial sketch, right third holds the symbol legend as left-aligned lines of text. Panel label '(a)' and '(b)' centered under each. In each sketch a tan wedge fills the lower right with its hypotenuse running from upper right to lower left at about 25–30 degrees; a gray line marks the slope surface. On the slope sit a tan block B with a smaller salmon block A on top, both drawn tilted to match the slope, with a thin black cord leaving A up-slope to the upper right. A rounded gray capsule outline encircles block A in panel (a) and block B in panel (b) to mark the isolated body. Free-body diagrams: a black dot on a short dashed line drawn at the incline angle; all force vectors are bold red arrows radiating from the dot, labeled in bold with overhead vector arrows. Panel (a) has four arrows (normal perpendicular up-left, tension up-slope, friction down-slope, weight straight down); panel (b) has five (normal up from incline, two friction arrows up-slope, one normal pressing down-right into the surface, weight straight down). Legends in black serif-style text repeat each symbol with its verbal definition. Interaction styling: the non-isolated body and its arrows drop to ~20% opacity; highlighted third-law pairs glow in a saturated accent (e.g. orange/gold stroke with a connecting curved annotation labelled 'equal and opposite, different bodies'); reversing the sliding tendency rotates each friction arrow 180 degrees along the dashed surface line while leaving normals and weights unchanged.
